articles.title_orig: Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal
articles.title_zh: Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal
articles.content_orig:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns any deal meeting Russia's demands could face European resistance.
President Donald Trump's push for a deal with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and potentially reshape European security has raised alarm among NATO allies, with a former top alliance commander warning Fox News Digital that President Vladimir Putin has long sought to divide the world into competing spheres of influence.
The warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also appeared to reject what he called a potential "Yalta 2.0," and NATO allies debated direct outreach to Putin ahead of delegations preparing for talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove , the former Supreme Allied Commander Europe, warned that Putin's ambitions extend far beyond Ukraine and reflect a broader vision for how global powers should divide influence.
"Putin has a plan for the world, and he has pushed that plan on leaders several times," Breedlove warned before adding: "He talks about it and he writes about it."
ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, front row from left, and Jonas Gahr Støre, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Ursula von der Leyen, Dutch Prime Minister Dick Schoof, and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, back row from left, stand together in the chancellery in Berlin, Germany, on Dec. 15, 2025. (Markus Schreiber, Pool/AP)
Trump had suggested Thursday that an agreement with Moscow could extend beyond ending Russia's nearly five-year war in Ukraine.
"It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... I could even say it might involve all of Europe," Trump told reporters after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.
"It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump added.
Breedlove said Putin has repeatedly promoted a vision of dividing global power among Russia, China and the United States.
"The plan is three spheres of influence whereby China controls the Far East, Russia controls Europe, and America controls the Western Hemisphere. I do not expect there's going to be a lot of cooperation from the countries of Europe," he said.
"The Western world is waiting to see what this big plan is, and they are very concerned because it is about them," Breedlove added.
President Donald Trump (R) and Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) hold a meeting at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Zelenskyy also warned Friday against repeating the 1945 Yalta Conference , where Allied leaders negotiated Europe's postwar order before the Soviet Union consolidated control over Eastern Europe.
"We don't want to have Yalta 2.0," the Ukrainian leader told CNN . "We don't want to be divided by Russia," he said before adding: "For me, it's not simple and it can be dangerous."
On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that discussions on how Europe would look after the Ukraine war were already underway.
"It's one of the key topics that's been raised repeatedly in every conversation, anytime negotiations have been discussed," he said ahead of traveling to Paris for the G7 meeting.
RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS
Secretary of State Marco Rubio talks to reporters at NATO Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, on Friday, April 4. (Jacquelyn Martin/Pool/AP)
"So I think that's what the president is alluding to, is that there's been some advances made and what that architecture could look like post-conflict. We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point," he added, clarifying Trump's comments.
Breedlove, however, questioned whether European governments and Ukraine would even accept a broader agreement negotiated without their involvement.
"I do expect that when we get a peek under the hood of what Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump have devised that there may be European partners and allies to include Ukraine that may or may not be enthralled with the proposed solution."
"We have always said nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," the expert said.
"Neither have we heard anything about the EU or NATO being in this conversation. And yet the EU, NATO and Ukraine are central and the heart of the matter that apparently is going to be discussed."
Tensions also appeared to mount further after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare 90-minute telephone conversation with Putin on Oct. 27, according to reports .
TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
A composite image shows Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (R) as peace talks continue. (Valery Sharifulin/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the separate European diplomatic initiatives.
"I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," she said as Breedlove went on to defend the outreach.
"The two calls that recently took place between Northern leaders in the NATO alliance and Russia, I don't think that they're out of place at all," he said. "I think they're entirely appropriate."
"The great powers of Europe are getting very concerned that someone is dealing with their security without including them in the conversation," he added.
Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Sunday that France would participate in the Abu Dhabi negotiations.
"The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions," Barrot said, according to Reuters.
FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT
President Donald Trump speaks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S., August 15, 2025. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
Breedlove warned that any agreement requiring European nations to sacrifice their security to satisfy Moscow would still face fierce resistance.
"If the maximalist demands of Russia remain intact and in order to find peace, all the rest of Europe has to give up its security, sacrifice its security, make itself more susceptible to Russian attack, then this is not going to go well," he said.
"Putin has never been a partner for peace in Ukraine. Putin is not now a partner for peace in Ukraine."
"The EU nations, the NATO nations, and Ukraine are not going to sign up to a plan that suggests that Russia will be able to once again amass its armies, march across borders and intervene in its neighbors' internal business."

articles.title_orig: Silverado's Dmitri Alperovitch on what's ahead for U.S.-China trade after Nvidia revelations
articles.title_zh: Silverado's Dmitri Alperovitch on what's ahead for U.S.-China trade after Nvidia revelations
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.
On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt  lingers.
It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.
Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.
CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.
It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.
"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.
"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."
"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."
Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.
The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."
— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
articles.content_orig:
Statement is rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.
Two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.
“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.
“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.
In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.
“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

articles.title_orig: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.title_zh: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.content_orig:
Bond yields had dropped for over a month starting in early October, providing much relief to bond investors walloped by the increase in yields in the first nine months of 2026. Recall that rising yields equate to falling bond prices, and vice versa.
But now yields are rising again. A nasty inflation surprise in the latest Consumer Price Index data released this week has led to heightened expectations of interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.
However, we remain optimistic about inflation coming down . And we believe that a slackening of artificial intelligence’s demand-side boost to the economy will ultimately push interest rates downward in 2027 and 2028, benefiting bond investors.
Bond yields have soared in 2026, with the two-year Treasury yield climbing by over 1.2 percentage points, to over 4.7% as of Nov. 11 from about 3.5% at the start of the year.
We’ve argued that the main force pushing bond yields higher has been the AI boom. The data center buildout is devouring capital, and AI spending and the concomitant uplift to stock prices are providing a broad demand-side boost to the economy. All of that has pushed interest rates up.
That’s not to say that other factors have played no role. Starting in mid-September, government debt worries helped push up yields for several weeks. That coincided with the spread between 10-year and two-year Treasury yields expanding by about 0.3 percentage points, which is what you expect given that debt sustainability is more of a long-term issue.
But the key role of AI asserted itself again starting in early October—this time on the downside. Disappointing hyperscaler earnings, along with a spotlight on the financial vulnerability of neocloud companies, triggered a cascade of worries that future AI spending would fall short of expectations. This showed up in declining stock prices in the tech sector, and it showed up in falling bond yields, validating our thesis about AI’s importance in driving the rise in bond yields in the first nine months of 2026.
The Democrats’ midterm wins provoked fears of restrictions on data center construction, leading to a further drop in bond yields in the days following the election.
From their recent peaks, the two-year and 10-year Treasury yields had fallen around half a percentage point by Nov. 5.
The downward trend in bond yields that started in early October ended on Nov. 10 when October CPI inflation came in higher than expected . The two-year Treasury yield jumped by around 0.2 percentage points on the day.
Yet bond market inflation expectations didn’t increase on the day, with the five-year breakeven yield (the difference between five-year Treasuries and five-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) staying flat. What did happen, however, is that expectations for federal-funds rate hikes climbed.
So the market isn’t worried about inflation getting out of control. But the market is worried that keeping inflation under control will require more rate hikes than previously expected.
Inflation in the Fed’s preferred PCE Price Index is likely to stand at 3.6% year-over-year as of October, well above the 2% inflation target.
We remain optimistic that inflation is ultimately going to come down without a massive further rise in interest rates. The fading tariff and energy price impact, along with subdued wage growth and housing inflation, should help push inflation down.
The key area of uncertainty about interest rates ultimately stems from AI’s demand-side boost to the economy. If the AI boom keeps expanding, the Fed could be forced to push interest rates much higher to keep the economy from overheating.
However, we think that AI’s demand-side boost is likely to fade . Either AI generates payoff on its massive investment via mass layoffs, or the lack of payoff forces a slowing of spending growth. Either scenario would be a negative demand shock, pushing interest rates downward.

articles.title_orig: House and Senate Republicans call on Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia - ABC News
articles.title_zh: House and Senate Republicans call on Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.
Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.
Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.
"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.
Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China .
Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.
The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.
By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."
And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk."  Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement  Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls
Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.
Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter  requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.
"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.
The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.
"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."
The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.
Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.
"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.

articles.title_orig: US Futures Gain With Microsoft Outage, Producer Prices in Focus
articles.title_zh: US Futures Gain With Microsoft Outage, Producer Prices in Focus
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
In a statement, Microsoft said the connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." The software giant said the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers.
Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday.
Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning.
In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online.
In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing.
Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.
Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete.
The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.
Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday.
Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.
The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.
Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.
U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress.
"Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said.
Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.
Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.
A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more.
Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.
The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.
"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."
"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.
Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.
Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."
At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.
"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq end lower as Nvidia uncertainty weighs on tech shares
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.
The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during the losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap and it pushed the company below Apple .
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.
Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair , this one with the company's vice president of health care.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.
"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.
Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.
In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.
Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."
"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls on Friday as Nvidia sells off, but index notches best week since August: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite fell on Friday as Nvidia shares added to their recent losses, though the index still notched a winning week alongside the other two major averages.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 0.91% to 25,136.27, while the S&P 500 slid 0.4% to 7,561.67. The Dow Jones Industrial Average eked out a gain of 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to end at 52,347.55.
Equities initially popped after October's producer price index reading — a measure of wholesale inflation — showed an increase of 0.3% on the month. Economists polled by Dow Jones had seen headline PPI rising 0.4%.
However, the report also showed producer prices gaining 6.5% from 12 months earlier — the biggest annual advance since November 2022.
Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market for another day. The stock fell 2% Friday, extending the more than 4% drop it saw in the previous session. The pressure came after the exit of the scandal-hit chipmaker's founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
HSBC downgraded the chipmaker Friday to hold, believing that the stock will languish until the company lays out a permanent succession plan.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
Thomas Martin of Globalt Investments expects the process of finding a new CEO to "take a lot of time" and spur even more uncertainty for the name.
"What will happen to those types of financing arrangements, and will there be less of them just going forward or will there actually be unwinding of them?" the senior portfolio manager told CNBC. "What are the relationships going to be with their suppliers and with their customers? It's just early days."
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all pulled back on Thursday after Huang stepped down from his post following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
To be sure, Baird's Ross Mayfield believes a lot of pain has already been priced into the stock, though he still anticipates volatility ahead. More broadly, he expects to see investors continue to rotate into non-AI corners of the market independent of the latest developments with Nvidia.
"Even before all of this came out, and even before the election, chip stocks had been under pressure. There had already been worries about a blue wave — worries about a Democratic sweep — [and] worries about the [return on investment] on all of this capex," the investment strategist said. "It hasn't really changed the broad tenor of the market."
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages notched weekly advances. The Nasdaq added 2.3%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.5%. The Dow gained 2.1%. All three indexes scored their best weekly performances since early August.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite finished in negative territory on Friday.
The broad market index fell 0.4% to 7,561.67, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 0.91% to 25,136.27.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to 52,347.55.
Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is scrambling the tech landscape as investors try to gauge the fallout for chip makers, neoclouds, and others in the artificial intelligence arms race.
The market has quickly passed judgement — bidding up shares of chipmakers like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom while pushing down neoclouds such as Coreweave and AI server maker Dell Technologies .
Traders can benefit from the volatility, but the market has a tendency to overshoot in both directions and estimates are changing rapidly. Long-term investors may want to wait until the dust settles.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
Apple shares climbed nearly 1% Friday, reaching an intraday record of $360.80, lifting the company's market value above $5.2 trillion.
The stock has benefited as investors move away from companies exposed to the AI infrastructure boom.
While many of its Magnificent Seven peers are committed to AI infrastructure buildouts, Apple has managed to stay away from the costly AI arms race. Bernstein analysts recently called Apple a "safe haven " and reiterated an outperform rating on Apple in the report, and a $380 price target, implying about 7% upside from Thursday's close.
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making big moves on Friday.
— Darla Mercado and Ananya Chetia
Cisco topped estimates on fiscal first-quarter earnings on Thursday, but Wall Street analysts are still somewhat measured on the outlook for the make of networking technologies amid the AI boom.
Tim Long at Barclays maintained his equal-weight rating on the stock in a Friday note, with a price target of $109 and potential upside of 6.9%.
"One area of weakness in the quarter was that hyperscaler AI orders were likely down meaningfully Q/Q in FQ1 based on our estimates, but these orders tend to be lumpy," he said.
Michael Ng at Goldman Sachs has a neutral rating on the stock, noting an "orders miss," per a Nov. 12 note.
"The margin outlook and upgrade was better-than-expected with CSCO demonstrating strong operating leverage, though growing hyperscale revenue mix may be headwinds to gross margin in F2H27," he said.
Nvidia is going to struggle until it gets a new CEO to permanently replace Jensen Huang and take over from CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress, according to HSBC.
Analyst Frank Lee downgraded the chipmaker to hold from buy. His price target of $170, down from $365, implies upside of just 2.3% from Thursday's close.
"We believe the uncertainties will prevail until a permanent succession plan is laid out and the new CEO is able to demonstrate execution capabilities," Lee said in a Friday note to clients.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Bitcoin traded below $70,000 for the first time since August in a risk-off move, falling as low as $67,632.68, its lowest level since Aug. 19, according to Coin Metrics.
Its recent weakness coincides with strength in the U.S. dollar. On Friday, the dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold – despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling and, this week, more than $1 billion in leveraged bitcoin liquidations, per CoinGlass. The declines began in late October, as concerns over AI valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off, and were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

articles.title_orig: Family Dollar to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers
articles.title_zh: Family Dollar to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers
articles.content_orig:
Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers by millions of dollars.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 U.S. states accused the budget retailer of failing to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in advertisements.
A proposed order bans Family Dollar from misleading customers on prices and requires the company to adopt what the FTC described as a "pricing accuracy program" that is independently assessed and certified annually.
"Today's order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Thursday.
Family Dollar operates more than 7,000 stores across 48 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. The Chesapeake, Virginia-based company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the settlement.
The FTC and the states' complaint alleged that pricing inaccuracies are widespread at Family Dollar stores and that the retailer failed to correct errors. Customers regularly reported being charged higher prices at the register than those displayed on goods' price tags, in stores, on the retailer's website and in its mobile app, according to the complaint.
The states include Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
In October, the FTC and 20 states sued another discount retailer, Dollar General , over allegations of similar deceptive pricing practices. The litigation is ongoing.
The proposed order requires Family Dollar to establish a $40 million fund to compensate eligible customers.
The retailer will notify customers of their eligibility for reimbursement through in-store notices and online. Eligible customers include anyone who made a purchase at a Family Dollar store from Jan. 1, 2023, to Oct. 1, 2026.
The order also establishes a separate $20 million discount program for customers. Under the program, Family Dollar must offer customers 15% off a range of goods for two days. State plaintiffs will receive $3 million to be divided among them.
The retailer must create a pricing accuracy program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices and trains employees to identify and correct pricing discrepancies.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
articles.title_zh: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.
Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.
Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.
"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.
Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China .
Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.
The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.
By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."
And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk."  Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement  Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls
Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.
Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter  requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.
"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.
The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.
"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."
The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.
Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.
"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock slips as investors digest CEO exit, broader chip sell-off accelerates
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock slips as investors digest CEO exit, broader chip sell-off accelerates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.
The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during the losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap and it pushed the company below Apple .
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.
Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair , this one with the company's vice president of health care.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.
"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.
Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.
In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.
Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."
"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

articles.title_orig: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
articles.title_zh: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
articles.content_orig:
Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday.
The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks.
"Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated.
The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling.
Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election.
Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed.
Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion.
The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

articles.title_orig: China & Taiwan Update, November 13, 2026
articles.title_zh: China & Taiwan Update, November 13, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
By WILIAM HUNTER, SENIOR SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY REPORTER
Published: 07:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 11:58 EST, 13 November 2026
If you are reading this, congratulations – you have survived the end of the world.
That is if a 1960 study predicting today to be ‘doomsday’ is to be believed – although with the Microsoft outage hitting offices, your day may still be a scene of panicked chaos as operations grind to a disastrous halt.
Conspiracy-minded commenters on social media have found a striking connection between the global disruption and a theory claiming ‘doomsday’ will occur on November 13, 2026.
One user cheekily suggested: 'Is it a mere coincidence? I don't think so... it was all planned.'
Written by Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American cybernetics expert, and two of his students, the study examined the last 2,000 years of human population growth and predicted it would ‘approach infinity’ and annihilate itself.
Writing in the journal Science, the trio argued: 'Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve. They will be squeezed to death.'
And with the supposed date of the apocalypse in mind, many commenters have pointed to their lack of emails as an ominous portent of doom.
Social media users have found a striking connection between this wacky prediction and the recent Microsoft outage
A doomsday event was predicted for today, Friday, November 13, 2026, by three scientists in 1960. Today, Microsoft servers are undergoing a global outage. Is it a mere coincidence? I don't think so .. it was all planned.
People have flocked to social media to share their wild conspiracy theories connecting the Microsoft outage to today's supposed apocalypse.
On X, one quipped: 'Is this the Doomsday November 13th that we all were talking about? @Microsoft.'
While another added: 'In 1960, scientists used a mathematical equation to predict that Friday, November 13, 2026 would be Doomsday. Nobody believed them until Outlook crashed globally this morning.'
Meanwhile, some conspiracy lovers made the connection to the traditionally unlucky date of Friday 13, as well as some other even stranger speculations.
One commenter wrote: 'It's Friday the 13th. Microsoft outage means no email. These seem related.'
While another asked: 'If astrology isn't real then why is the Microsoft outage happening on the last day of Mercury Retrograde?'
In reality, Professor von Foerster's theory has long since been debunked and doesn't have the slightest connection to today's internet outages.
In 1960, one of the world's leading scientific journals published a paper suggesting that the population would surge toward infinity (illustrated), leading to 'doomsday' on Friday, November 13, A.D. 2026
So Doomsday was predicted back in 1960s for November 13th 2026. And all of a sudden Microsoft down. Summin ain’t adding up 🧐 https://t.co/rGvIjLwR4v
Professor Alan MacEachern, a professor of history at Western University, pointed out that the 1960 calculations were based on a fundamental error.
Writing in The Conversation, he noted that the global birth rate is now significantly lower than it was when the article was published.
This suggests the prediction of doomsday on November 13 is based on outdated figures.
‘Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts,’ Professor MacEachern explained.
‘Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.’
That means there’s no need for anyone to worry about being ‘squeezed to death’.
Professor MacEachern also points out that the lead author, Heinz von Foerster, was a stage magician at one point in his life.
As a result, the scientist may have used elements of his tricks in his paper.
Microsoft users continued to experience disruption today as the tech giant worked to resolve outages impacting some of its most popular services
'Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal,' Professor MacEachern explained.
'Von Foerster and his co–authors' article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion.
'It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.
'To draw the world's attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity — that's a good trick.'
That means there's no need for anyone to worry about being 'squeezed to death'.
On the other hand, the ongoing Microsoft outage appears to be related to an internal issue with the company's internal infrastructure.
In several notices posted on social media, Microsoft said it was investigating the disruptions and suggested the problems could be down to parts of its infrastructure 'experiencing elevated load'.
Microsoft determined a number of servers failed during automated health checks and that its alternatives to bring those servers back online were not immediately taking effect.
Likewise, experts have ruled out the possibility of a cyber-attack disrupting the tech giant's services.
Mantas Sasnauskas, cyber-security researcher and editor-in-chief of Ransomnews , told the Daily Mail: 'Nothing so far points to a cyberattack. Microsoft says it is not aware of any malicious activity, and what it has described fits that.
'Servers dropped out and then failed again as soon as traffic came back. A denial-of-service attack looks like a flood of hostile traffic. This looks like a failure inside the platform.'
However, as Microsoft battles to bring systems back online, the company has acknowledged that efforts to restore services were 'not taking as expected'.
Millions of users around the world began reporting that Outlook was down shortly after 6pm GMT on Thursday, in what experts have dubbed the 'most disruptive email-related business outage of all time'.
More than 14 hours later, users are still unable to open their inboxes, send emails and access other Microsoft services.
Governments, police forces and numerous companies around the world have reported problems with their services, but no definitive cause has been given.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang was a ‘China salesman’ for Nvidia. His exit is weighing on Chinese tech stocks.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang was a ‘China salesman’ for Nvidia. His exit is weighing on Chinese tech stocks.
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co- founded.
Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.
Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.
"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.
Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China .
Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.
The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.
By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."
And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk."  Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement  Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls
Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.
Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford, R-Ark., send a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter  requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast sent a second request to Kessler.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.
"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.
The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.
"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."
The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.
Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.
"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.
